title: Five years: the long story
tomorrow: a raga, a rule or a line: what changed Simran most?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the banis: seven lines on a school bus, from aad sach to balihaari gur aapne, a day held at both ends. Today, Bebe gets out the photos.

Saturday morning, and the kitchen table is covered in photographs with curled corners. Simran came in for chilies and got stuck. Bebe holds up one: a man in a turban beside a farm truck, squinting into the Central Valley sun. Your great-grandfather, she says. He drove, like your dad drives. Simran asks where the story starts, expecting a port, a ship, an airport. Bebe shakes her head. Kartarpur, she says. A village on a riverbank. Start there.
screen: `PHOTOS WITH CURLED CORNERS.` → `A TURBAN BY A FARM TRUCK.` → `START IN KARTARPUR.`

segments.voice: Tradition says that after years on the road, Guru Nanak settled at Kartarpur, by the Ravi river, and farmed. People came to sing with him, eat with him and work the fields. That's the long story's first scene: not a palace, a farm with a shared kitchen. Then the light passes from Guru to Guru. Towns grow around them. Amritsar and its pool. The Khalsa at Anandpur. And there are martyrs, people who gave their lives rather than give up their faith. Sikhs don't keep that part in a museum. They pray it. Ardas, the prayer that closes almost any Sikh gathering, remembers the Gurus, the Guru's sons, the five beloved ones and the martyrs, by name and by deed. Then, much later in the long story, families leave Punjab: for cities, for ships, for farms half a world away, carrying the Granth with them. That's how a riverbank village reaches a California kitchen. Now the part to tell a friend tonight. After all that remembering, Ardas ends with two wishes: chardi kala, rising spirits, and sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not the good of Sikhs. The good of everyone. Simran looks at the man by the truck for a long time.
screen: `A FARM BY THE RAVI.` · `GURU TO GURU, TOWN TO TOWN.` · `ARDAS REMEMBERS THE MARTYRS.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `THE LONG STORY.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes. If you know Ardas, say quietly the part that remembers those who gave their lives; if not, bring to mind the names from this week's stories, one at a time, and let each one go by slowly. End where Ardas ends: sarbat da bhala, the good of all.
Five years: the long story. From Guru Nanak's farm at Kartarpur to a kitchen table in California, remembered every day in Ardas.
Your line: the long story, and it ends on the good of all. One photo is on Simran's phone now.

howItsDone: Ardas is said standing, often with folded hands, at the close of Sikh services and at home; it remembers the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Pyare and the martyrs, and ends asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape story (Bebe's photos; the scene opens mid-morning and the teach answers 'where does the story start?').
For parents: Ardas remembers martyrs; the voice says only 'people who gave their lives rather than give up their faith' and gives no details of how they died.
Unity thread: Ardas closes with 'sarbat da bhala', the good of all; the voice adds 'not the good of Sikhs. The good of everyone.' Confirm this reading is fair (it is the common understanding).
Kartarpur 'by the Ravi', settled after his travels, farming: tradition (janamsakhis); told with 'tradition says'. Amritsar, Anandpur named without dates.
'Ardas, the prayer that closes almost any Sikh gathering': softened sweeping claim; confirm or soften further.
Outline hook says 'to every continent'; the voice avoids the claim and says 'farms half a world away'. Simran's great-grandfather driving a farm truck in the Central Valley is storyline, not history.
2026-10-15: new lesson recipe data (chat, gloss, recall) written with the lesson (job 3 recipe); confirm the chat reply, glosses, scripts and pronunciations with the Keeper.
